rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s opening conjunction links this reflection to the preceding warning about the Resurrection, answering deniers by directing attention to ordinary visible signs of the Creator’s power.
rows.anchor: Yukarıya bir tefrî‘olan bu cümlenin fâ ile rabtındaki mâna gāşiye hadîsini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder completes the earlier surah’s call to purification: creation’s signs are studied to infer divine ways and commands and to prompt useful deeds before the closing command to remind.
rows.anchor: suhuf-i ûlâda olduğu anlatılan tezekkî mazmûnunun suhuf-i uhrâda mütemmim ve mükemmili

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who prefer worldly life should inspect creation to understand their end and seek works that bring lasting satisfaction rather than fruitless effort.
rows.anchor: dünyayı âhirete tercih eden gāfiller hâlâ önünü sonunu görmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Starting with the camel is apt because the aim is to show marvels even in familiar, apparently commonplace things, and the camel is especially familiar to Arabs.
rows.anchor: maksad bakılması mu‘tad olan ve pek âdî gibi görünen şeylerin bile keyfiyet-i hilkatleri acâibât ile meşhun bulunduğunu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from bedding to camel, then sky, mountains, and the earth creates a remarkable survey whose changing sounds and expansiveness suit the aim of displaying creation’s wonders.
rows.anchor: serilmiş döşeklerden bir lahzada deveye atlatarak ondan semâya, ondan cibâle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel’s unusual size, strength, form, sparse diet, endurance without water, posture, and ability to travel under heavy loads are signs of astonishing creation.
rows.anchor: Birçok hayvanların hilkatine benzemeyen iri cüssesi, şiddetli kuvveti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite its strength, the camel is obedient to human direction, remembers routes exceptionally well, and responds eagerly to the singer’s call.
rows.anchor: en zayıf bir hayvandan, bir koyundan, bir merkebten daha ziyade ve hatta bir çocukla bile yedilip güdülebilecek derecede itaat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparing human bodily weakness with the camel’s power and human mastery over it should lead people to recognize the Creator’s power, particularizing will, ordering command, and their own moral destination.
rows.anchor: İnsan kendi zekâsıyla bu acîb hilkat arasındaki fark ve münasebeti düşünür

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel makes especially clear how spiritual knowledge and insight can govern material force, and beginning with it is useful for everyone.
rows.anchor: ilm ü marifet gibi mânevî kuvvetlerin maddî kuvvetlere tefevvuk ve hâkimiyetini sarih bir misâl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the elephant is larger and also remarkable, it is less suitable because it is not as clean, visible, or familiar to Arabs as the camel, their most valuable possession.
rows.anchor: büyüktür ve onun hilkatinde de bâriz bir acîblik vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Looking at the camel just after the mention of darīʿ has an additional rhetorical suitability.
rows.anchor: “darî‘”in zikrinden sonra deveye bir atf-ı nazar etmenin de başkaca bir münasebet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riding a camel raises the traveler high enough to see the sky, mountains, and earth, and wider, deeper observation expands knowledge of creation, blessings, the future, and the value of effort.
rows.anchor: seyr ü sefer etmek üzere deveye binen bir kimse boyundan hayli yüksek bir irtifâ‘a çıkmış olur

rows.speaker: Ebu’l-Abbas Müberred
rows.claim: Müberred regarded the transition from looking at the camel to the sky as too remote and sought a more homogeneous relation between the coordinated objects.
rows.anchor: Ebu’l-Abbas Müberred gibi bazıları burada deveye

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: The Kashshāf author allows a metaphorical reading of “camels” as clouds because Arabic poetry compares clouds to camels; he does not claim it is a regular cloud-name.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf der ki: “Bunun murâdı ‘ibil’in ‘gamâm’, ‘müzn’, ‘rebab’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the need for metaphor: moving from the camel to the sky is natural and graceful guidance for Arabs whose valleys, deserts, and journeys center on camels.
rows.anchor: Fakat mecaza hâcet yoktur. Deveye nazardan semâya nazara geçirmek bilhassa vâdilerinde

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ignoring the camel’s extraordinary creation is heedlessness, but riding it while failing to contemplate the sky and the Creator is an even greater heedlessness.
rows.anchor: Deve en istifadeli malı olup da ona bakmamak, acîb hilkatini düşünmemek nasıl büyük gaflet ise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky is a wondrous, vast height above the air, adorned with innumerable celestial bodies moving in their courses without visible supports.
rows.anchor: her biri bir felekte direksiz dayaksız yüzüp duran lâ-yu‘ad ecrâm ve kevâkibiyle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains rise from the ground toward the sky, bound the view, and provide varied benefits; their placement and fixing invite reflection.
rows.anchor: dağlara yerden o semâya doğru ser çekerek dikilip nazarları tahdid

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth is the submissive dwelling people inhabit and will enter at death; its plains, seas, valleys, and mountains have been leveled into a surface fit for life and travel.
rows.anchor: O dağlar, vâdilerle beraber ovalar denizler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflection on earth, sky, mountains, and the earth’s changing formation should establish the Creator’s power, resurrection, recompense, and the need to work for the true path.
rows.anchor: Bütün bunlara tedebbür ve ibret nazarıyla bakıp da yaradanın kudretini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth is a temporary home for human life, death, and resurrection, so people should understand their dwelling and consider the end of those who denied truth.
rows.anchor: Arz insanlar için bir zamana kadar hayattan nasib alınacak bir yurttur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an directs people to travel the earth and consider the fate of deniers, rather than spend life in ignorant or futile pursuits.
rows.anchor: قُلْ سِيرُوا۟ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ ٱنظُرُوا۟ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلْمُكَذِّبِينَ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These signs are summarized rather than explained in detail because they are observable realities whose particulars can be discovered through human inquiry and study.
rows.anchor: yalnız halk, ref‘, nasb, satıh keyfiyetlerine icmâlen nazar-ı dikkat celbolunmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Close observation and experiment can yield knowledge of animals, astronomy, geography, earth’s layers, and natural history; such inquiry is a divine aim and useful for Muslims.
rows.anchor: hayvânât, hey’et, coğrafya, tabakāt-ı Arz ve târîh-i tabîî denilen aklî ve tecribî ilimlerin fâidelerine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Empirical sciences should serve recognition of the Creator’s actions, signs, and laws, refutation of false beliefs, and preparation for the afterlife, rather than become an ultimate end.
rows.anchor: bunları gāye-i marifet addetmeyip Hâlık’ın tasarrufâtı keyfiyetleriyle kudreti âyâtını ve kanunlarını tanımak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Peoples who best understand the earth and its life-rules and act on that knowledge have prevailed over idle pleasure-seeking peoples and ignorant, aggressive ones.
rows.anchor: Arz’ı ve ahvâlini ve Arz üzerinde hayat kāidelerini en iyi bilenler ve bilgileri nisbetinde iyi çalışan milletler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who choose worldly life and those who do not all eventually leave it; lasting felicity belongs to those who work for the afterlife with faith, knowledge, sincerity, certainty, and good deeds.
rows.anchor: iman ve irfan ve ihlâs ve îkān ile âhiret için çalışan ve güzel amellerle Hakk’a kavuşanlar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The required reflection may be concise or detailed: the verses give a summary, while detailed discovery is entrusted to observation and investigation.
rows.anchor: Şüphe yok ki bu nazar icmâlî de tafsîlî de olabilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Observable, summarized signs of creation are called reminders because their causes of knowledge are already rooted in human reason and can be found through rational and experimental inquiry.
rows.anchor: böyle icmâlen vâki‘olan işârât-ı ilâhiyeye “tezkir” nâmı verilmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed fā draws the consequence: if they still do not look and think, the Prophet should remind them through preaching and warning and convey the need and results of reflection.
rows.anchor: O hâlde tezkir et yani hâlâ bakmıyorlar, bunlara nazar edip düşünmüyorlarsa sen onlara va‘z u nasihat ile hatırlat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s task is only to deliver and remind; he should not try to force people to think or compel them to believe.
rows.anchor: tezkir ile iktifâ et de daha ziyade zorlama, zorla düşündüreceğim diye uğraşma

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being no overpowering master means the Prophet cannot compel their reflection, control their hearts, or make them adopt a belief as he wishes.
rows.anchor: Zorla nazar ettirip düşündürecek, her istediğin şeyi yaptıracak, kalblerine hükmedip

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is supported by the statement that the Prophet does not guide whom he loves.
rows.anchor: إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِى مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who turn away, refuse the warning, and persist in disbelief will therefore be punished by God with the greatest punishment, the punishment of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: Ancak her kim aksine gidip küfür ederse yani tezkir ve ihtârı dinlemez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife’s punishment is greater than worldly punishment; a worldly punishment may be added but remains small by comparison.
rows.anchor: Ona bazen dünya azâbı dahi munzam olursa da o âhiret azâbına nisbetle küçük kalır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: However far they turn or flee, all return to God, who alone will reckon with them; they will answer to Him and cannot escape the greatest punishment.
rows.anchor: ne kadar kaçmaya çalışsalar âkıbet dönüp Bize geleceklerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next surah elaborates the lesson of these reflections by drawing attention to changes in time while explaining the final return to God.
rows.anchor: Allah’a rücû‘âkıbetinin bir tavzîhi siyâkında zaman tehavvülâtına dikkati celb ile başlayan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the pillars, tents, or Iram; the clearest reading is that Iram was an unparalleled city, while unmatched stature or strength among its people is possible but less immediate.
rows.anchor: bir belde olmasında zâhirdir. O kavmin kuvvet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No likeness was created” means that nothing like it had been made up to that time.
rows.anchor: Misli yaratılmamış olması da o zamana kadar demek olmalıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Thamud cut rock in the valley to build their houses; this power and craft were gifts God gave them.
rows.anchor: Bu suretle kendilerine evler yapıyorlardı ki bu Allah’ın onlara vermiş olduğu bir kuvvet ve san‘at idi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb javb means cutting through something as if slicing it, and it can also mean traversing a distance.
rows.anchor: “Cevb” bir şeyi yaka biçer gibi kesip biçmektir. Mesafe kat‘etmeye de “cevb” tâbir olunur

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they traveled through lands and carved houses, pools, and buildings to their liking from mountains and rocks.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas demiştir ki: “Beldeleri dolaşırlar ve

rows.speaker: Mukātil
rows.claim: Muqatil identifies the valley as Wadi al-Qura.
rows.anchor: Mukātil demiştir ki: “‘Vâdî’ Vâdi’l-kurâ’dır.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says the Thamud were the first to carve mountains, rocks, and marble, making about 1,700 cities, all of stone.
rows.anchor: bin yedi yüz kadar medine yapmışlardı, hepsi taştan idi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says they cut channels in their valley and directed water into a reservoir carved inside a rock.
rows.anchor: vâdilerini kesmişler, sularını yonttukları bir kayanın içine mahzen hâlinde celbetmişlerdi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Genealogists identify Thamud as a famous extinct Arab tribe and offer differing ancestry traditions; the commentator leaves the genealogy uncertain.
rows.anchor: Nessâbûnun zikrettikleri bu neseb, sahih olsun olmasın

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Thamud’s known homes were at al-Hijr between Syria and the Hijaz, and their destruction is recounted in multiple surahs.
rows.anchor: Areb’de Semûd ve Şam ile Hicaz arasında Hicr’de menzilleri mâruftur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awtād is the plural of watad, “stake”; the Qur’an also calls mountains stakes, and the image conveys strength and firmness.
rows.anchor: “Evtâd” mâlum ki “veted”in cem‘i olup kazıklar demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description “possessor of stakes” resembles the idiom of wanting to drive a stake into the world, expressing the wish to establish oneself permanently.
rows.anchor: Bu tâbir, bizim “dünyaya kazık kakmak istiyor” tâbirimizin de menşe’i gibidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes take the stakes as Pharaoh’s numerous soldiers and tent pegs, his cruel punishments, or his firm kingdom and powerful men; a poet’s phrase illustrates the latter.
rows.anchor: Askerinin ve kondukları yerlerde çaktıkları çadır kazıklarının çokluğu

rows.speaker: Katâde
rows.claim: In a report from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, the stakes were amusements under which entertainers performed for Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: Katâde’nin Saîd b. Cübeyr’den rivayetinde de “o evtâd birtakım melâ‘ib idi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most evident meaning to the author is the pyramids known in Egypt, which visually resemble stakes driven into the earth.
rows.anchor: en açık olarak anlayabileceğimiz mâna, bu evtâd Mısır’da mâruf olan dağ gibi ehramlara işaret olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s claim to rule Egypt and ownership of pyramids displayed an ambition and power to drive stakes into the world; Moses’ Pharaoh represents the whole institution of Pharaohs.
rows.anchor: diyen Firavun bu ehramlara sâhip bulunuyor ve bunlarla dünyaya kazık kakmak istediklerini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pyramids were not public benefactions but playgrounds built for Pharaohs’ pleasure, and many performances took place beneath them.
rows.anchor: firavunların zulümleriyle keyifleri için oynanmış melâ‘ib demektir

rows.speaker: Şeyh Abduh
rows.claim: Abduh says the enduring Egyptian buildings are aptly called stakes: pyramids look driven into earth, and the sections of great statues also resemble inverted stakes.
rows.anchor: Mısırlı Şeyh Abduh demiştir ki: “Mısırlıların bıraktıkları ebniye-i bâkiyeden ‘evtâd’ ile tâbir ne güzeldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pillars of ʿĀd, the carved rocks of Thamud, and Pharaoh’s stakes portray powerful people with long ambitions who sought to anchor themselves in the world.
rows.anchor: İşte Âd o imâdları, Semûd o kestikleri kayaları, Firavun bu kazıkları ile dünyaya kazık kakmak isteyen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proud of their strength and ruled by desire, these peoples exceeded the bounds of justice and violated the rights of people and their Creator.
rows.anchor: hak ve adalet hudûdunu aşıp halkın ve Hâlık’ın hukūkuna tasallut ve tecavüzde ileri gitmişlerdi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They multiplied corruption both within and beyond their lands through oppression, waste, and debauchery, damaging order, morals, and ideas.
rows.anchor: Zulüm, israf, sefâhetle çok fesad yapmış; nizâmı, ahlâkı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God poured successive, severe blows of punishment upon each people, like repeatedly raining down lashes.
rows.anchor: azabdan bir kamçıyı döker, yağdırır gibi şiddet ve tevâlî ile indirip mütevâlî darbelerle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawt originally means mixing and came to denote a whip braided from intertwined strands; varied punishments are likened to repeated whip blows and expressed as being poured down.
rows.anchor: “Sevt”, aslında karıştırmak mânasına masdar olup deriden örülmüş katları birbirine karıştırılmış olan kamçıda

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite “punishment” signals that the punishment inflicted on each people differed.
rows.anchor: Azâbın nekre olması ile de her birine olan azâbın başkalığına işaret kılınmıştır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirsād literally names a place where watchers keep watch; the commentator connects the term with Hell described as a watchpost.
rows.anchor: “Mirsâd” râsıdların rasad ettikleri, gözettikleri

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse uses a parabolic metaphor: God watches every servant like a vigilant observer, misses nothing, and recompenses each according to deeds.
rows.anchor: Kelâmda isti‘âre-i temsîliye vardır. Yani seni yetiştiren, her işini tedbir eden Rabbin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This clause either confirms the oath’s answer or explains the punishment; rebels should not imagine they can escape God or His punishment.
rows.anchor: Bu cümle kasemin cevâbını tekid veya ta‘zîbi ta‘lîldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Lord watches people’s striving for the afterlife, people ought to work for His approval.
rows.anchor: Rabbinin şânı bu: Kullarının âhiret için sa‘yini gözetir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heedless person watches worldly pleasures: God’s testing assigns duties and makes a person accountable in the afterlife according to performance.
rows.anchor: mükellef kılar, ibraz edeceği hâle göre âhirette mes’ul etmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honor means bringing someone forward with worldly status, while bestowing abundant blessings means increasing provision and wealth.
rows.anchor: hoşuna gidecek ikbal ve câh ile yüze çıkarır

rows.speaker: Ebussuud
rows.claim: Ebussuud, followed by Alusi, treats the fā before “honored him” as explanatory, making honor and blessing identical with the trial.
rows.anchor: Ebussuud ve ona tebe‘an Âlûsî فَأَكْرَمَهُۥ’da “fâ”yı tefsîriye addetmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that analysis: the fā is causal, and the honor and blessing are specifically granted through the trial and its duties, so the two expressions differ.
rows.anchor: fikrimizce bu doğru değildir. Bu فَا sebebiye olmalıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heedless person treats trial-bound worldly favor as unconditional honor, imagines himself permanently beloved, ignores accountability, and falls into pleasure-seeking, excess, corruption, and loss.
rows.anchor: Kendisini Allah’ın ilelebed mükrem kıldığı sevgili kullarından imiş gibi farzeder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is narrated as a future divine saying, preparing the listener for that day; the believer had already found tranquility through faith, sincerity, and offering good to God.
rows.anchor: Bu üslûb-i ifade Kur’ân’ın i‘câzı tarzlarından birisidir. Bunda sâmi‘i derhâl istikbâle hazırlayacak bir telkin vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tranquil soul returns content with its Lord and accepted by Him, echoing the reciprocal satisfaction of God and the believers.
rows.anchor: sen Rabbinden hoşnut, Rabbin de senden hoşnut

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering God’s servants means joining the sincere, distinguished, righteous servants devoted to Him.
rows.anchor: Bana ihlâs ile kulluk eden, Bana ihtisas ile temayüz eyleyen hâlis ibâd-ı sâlihîn zümresine katıl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation has the soul join the ranks of the near ones and shine through their light as pure spirits reflect one another.
rows.anchor: Mukarrebîn sırasına dizil ve onların nûrlarıyla parla

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation understands the entry as the soul entering bodies and then entering the abode of reward with them.
rows.anchor: Cesetlere gir, onlarla birlikte dâr-ı sevâba gir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafs basically means a thing’s own essence; for a person it is the self that says “I” and has unified awareness through different states.
rows.anchor: “nefs” bir şeyin kendisi denilen zât ve hakikatidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self has both perceiving and perceived aspects; in sleep, heedlessness, fainting, or death those aspects may be considered apart, and nafs can name either sentient desire or rational discerning spirit.
rows.anchor: biri duyan, şâ‘ir, biri de duyulan, meş‘ur olmak üzere iki haysiyeti hâizdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self’s unity is grounded in the higher reality of God, who comes between a person and their heart and gathers people to Him.
rows.anchor: insanın nefsine intıbâkı, cihet-i vahdeti kendisinde değil, kendisinin fevkinde bir hakikattedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spirit is from the Lord’s command, and God takes souls at death and during sleep; separation from ordinary awareness is return to God, not annihilation.
rows.anchor: mısdâkınca rûh, emr-i Rab olduğu gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators take nafs here to mean the self or essence, while others take it to mean the spirit; mutmainna can accordingly describe either.
rows.anchor: Burada çokları zât mânasına bazıları da rûh mânasına telakkī etmişlerdir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi’s first account of tranquility is attaining certainty in the truth that no doubt can disturb, as in Abraham’s request for his heart to be reassured.
rows.anchor: Birincisi, hiçbir şüphe ile bulanmayacak vechile hakka yakīn zevkine ermektir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi’s second account is security from fear and grief, promised at death, resurrection, and entry into Paradise.
rows.anchor: havf ü hüzünden sarsılmayacak vechile emniyet hâsıl etmektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third account of tranquility is that hearts rest only through remembrance of God, as both Qur’an and rational proof establish.
rows.anchor: bu itmi’nân ancak zikrullah ile olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi’s first rational proof says the intellect keeps seeking a cause beyond every contingent cause until it reaches the Necessary Existent, where it can rest.
rows.anchor: tâ bütün hâcetlerin kesildiği ve bütün zarûretlerin müntehî olduğu vücûdu kendinden, lizâtihî Vâcibü’l-vücûd’a müntehî oluncaya kadar gider

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi’s second proof says humans have limitless needs but finite things cannot meet them; tranquility therefore requires God’s limitless perfection.
rows.anchor: abdin nihâyetsiz olan hâceti mukabilinde Allah’ın nihâyetsiz olan kemâli lâzımdır ki istikrar hâsıl olabilsin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tranquil soul chooses knowledge of God for God alone and is attached to Him in love, desire, abiding, and speech.
rows.anchor: her kim ma‘rifetullâhı onun gayri bir şey için olmayarak ihtiyar ederse işte o nefs-i mutmainnedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tranquil soul is defined by rising through unstable causes to know the First Source, relying only on God, and obeying Him with exclusive sincerity.
rows.anchor: esbâb ve müsebbebât silsilelerinden geçip bizzat müessir olan Mebde’-i A‘lâ’yı mârifete yükselerek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This definition entails submission to God with excellence, certainty of release from fear and sorrow, and dedicating the self to seek only God’s pleasure.
rows.anchor: Allah için İslâm ve ihsan ile havf u hüzünden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True freedom means escaping the animal ego, self-reproach, and bondage to anything besides God, then doing every good one can with life and wealth in God’s path.
rows.anchor: nefs-i emmâre tekāzâsından, nefs-i levvâme melâmetinden, mâsivâya esaret kaydlarından kurtarıp

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas defines the tranquil soul as one that confirms the truth.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’tan: Nefs-i mutmainne, musaddıka

rows.speaker: Katâde
rows.claim: Qatadah describes it as assured by God’s promise and confirming His word.
rows.anchor: Katâde’den: Allah’ın vaadine mutmain, kavlini musaddık

rows.speaker: Mücâhid
rows.claim: Mujahid says it is certain that God is its Lord and submits to His command in every deed.
rows.anchor: Mücâhid’den: Allah, rabbi olduğunu musaddık mûkın ve her yaptığı işte O’nun emrine müslim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another formulation says the soul is certain God is its Lord, gives its heart only to Him, and has a heart that beats by His command; it is repentant and humble.
rows.anchor: Allah rabbi olduğuna îkān etmiş, gönlünü ancak O’na vermiş, kalbi O’nun emriyle çarpar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports describing certainty of meeting God and a heart beating with longing for Him also point to the complementary Qur’anic descriptions of believers and the humble.
rows.anchor: yekdiğerini mütemmim olan târiflerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi writers discuss the soul’s ranks, stations, and states; Sufism as a whole revolves around the maxim that knowing oneself leads to knowing one’s Lord.
rows.anchor: Hatta bütün tasavvuf مَنْ عَرَفَ نـَفْسَهُ فـَقَدْ عَرَفَ رَبَّهُ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufis enumerate seven soul-states: commanding, self-reproaching, tranquil, content, accepted, inspired, and purified.
rows.anchor: Nefs-i emmâre, nefs-i levvâme, nefs-i mutmainne, nefs-i râzıye, nefs-i marziyye

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding account contrasts the ignorant, worldly commanding soul and belatedly self-reproaching soul with the tranquil soul that understood truth in time.
rows.anchor: nefs-i emmâre ve nefs-i levvâme hükümleri gösterilmiş, sonra da vaktiyle hakkı anlayıp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes differ on whether this address comes at death, resurrection, or after the reckoning; the author considers the last timing most apparent from the context.
rows.anchor: Bunda üç kavil vardır: Ölüm zamanında olması, ba‘s zamanında

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the preferred timing, returning means leaving the place of reckoning for the place God graciously commands, or turning the heart from concern over acceptance to God Himself.
rows.anchor: hesab görülen mevkıften Allah teâlâ’nın inayet ve ikramıyla emir buyurduğu mahalle demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pleased soul is content with the Lord who brought it to eternal bliss; the accepted soul is approved by God for its sound heart and good striving and reaches divine pleasure.
rows.anchor: marziyye de Rabbin indinde marzî ve makbul; yani selîm kalbin, güzel sa‘y ü amelin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fā in “enter among My servants” is explanatory, clarifying what returning means.
rows.anchor: fâ, tefsîriye olarak rücû‘u beyandır

rows.speaker: İkrime
rows.claim: Ikrima and Dahhak report that the address and command to return occur at resurrection; on this reading the soul returns to its Lord for eternal life.
rows.anchor: İkrime ve Dahhâk’ten rivayet olunduğuna göre bu hitab ile ٱرْجِعِىٓ emri ba‘s sırasındadır

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: On the resurrection reading, commentators who understand nafs as spirit interpret entering among the servants as the spirit returning to its separated body, a report also attributed to Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: bunun İbn Abbas’tan ve İbn Cübeyr’den mervî olduğunu da söylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, entering God’s garden means entering the abode of reward together with the servants.
rows.anchor: birlikte dâr-ı sevab olan cennete duhûldür

rows.speaker: İbn Zeyd
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and many others hold that the address is spoken at the time of death.
rows.anchor: İbn Zeyd ve daha birçokları da bu hitâbın mevt sırasında söyleneceğine kāil olmuşlardır

rows.speaker: İbn Cübeyr
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr reports that when this verse was recited before Abu Bakr, the Prophet told him an angel would say it to him at death.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem de أَمَا إِنَّ الْمَلَكَ سَيـَقُولُ لَكَ عِنْدَ الْمَوْتِ

rows.speaker: Hakîm-i Tirmizî
rows.claim: Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmits a similar report from Abu Bakr through Sulaym ibn Amir.
rows.anchor: b. Aclân tarîkiyle Selim b. Âmir’den, Hazret-i Sıddîk radıyallâhu anh’tan rivayet eylemiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the address occurs at death, nafs means spirit and returning is the spirit’s departure from the body toward its Lord.
rows.anchor: Bu surette “nefs” rûh mânasına olup rücû‘u rûhun bedenden iftirâkıyla Rabbine doğru

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the death reading, the fā may indicate immediate joining of the near spirits in the spirit-world or joining the righteous after resurrection.
rows.anchor: bilâ terahî âlem-i ervâhta mukarrebîn silkine duhûl veya sonra ba‘s ile sâlihîn zümresine duhûl

rows.speaker: Ebû Sâlih
rows.claim: Abu Salih says returning to the Lord is at death as departure from the world, while entering among the servants and entering Paradise are commands at resurrection.
rows.anchor: Bu âyette ٱرْجِعِىٓ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ inde’l-mevttir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though Abu Salih’s reading seems apparent, the context favors the address after resurrection and completed reckoning; the reports can fit by treating each death as a person’s resurrection or the commands together as a unit.
rows.anchor: bu hitâbın da o güne ait olması iktizâ edeceğinden ba‘de’l-ba‘s

rows.speaker: Zeyd b. Eslem
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam reports that the tranquil soul is given this address at death, resurrection, and the gathering, and is promised Paradise.
rows.anchor: mutmainne ölüm sırasında ve ba‘s sırasında ve cem‘günü cennet ile tebşir olunmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority understand an omitted “God will say” from the preceding context, making the address and commands declarative and creative rather than legislative.
rows.anchor: cumhûrun muhtârı budur. Buna göre bu hitâbın ve emirlerin teşrî‘î değil tekvînî olması

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author also considers a direct, legislative divine address at the surah’s conclusion plausible; separation from what precedes highlights that the tranquil souls themselves should hear it.
rows.anchor: bunun nüfûs-i mutmainne tarafından re’sen ve bilhassa istimâ‘ı maksud olduğuna tenbih için

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the address as applying to the tranquil soul in worldly life at all times; the author finds this clearer and more useful.
rows.anchor: bir kısım müfessirîn de bunun nefs-i mutmainneye dünyada da her zaman için hitab olduğuna kāil olmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the worldly reading, returning is a voluntary return to God and His decree in every matter, accompanied by contentment in prosperity and adversity.
rows.anchor: rücû‘ile emir rücû‘-i irâdî olarak her işte ve bütün umûrunda râzıye olmak kaydıyla Allah teâlâ’ya

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explicit contentment is difficult even for the tranquil soul and is the perfection of the content soul; divine acceptance depends on that contentment.
rows.anchor: bu mertebe nefs-i mutmainnenin kemâli mertebesi olan nefs-i râzıye hasleti olduğu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causative fā commands worldly effort to increase righteous deeds, join God’s sincere servants free of Satan’s dominion, and belong to their group in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: dünyada rızâullâha muvâfık a‘mâl-i sâlihayı çoğaltarak üzerlerinde Şeytan’ın sultası olmayan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering God’s garden means entering Paradise with those servants in the hereafter, signaling the tranquil soul’s good final outcome.
rows.anchor: âhirette onlarla beraber cennete dâhil olmak ile emir olmuş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The life of a tranquil soul among the righteous is like the ten nights before Eid al-Adha, and its entry into Paradise is the dawn of the greatest festival of bliss.
rows.anchor: dünya ömrü îd-i adhâya tekaddüm eden bir leyâl-i aşr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentator prays that he and his readers return to God content and accepted, join His sincere servants, and reach Paradise and the vision of God.
rows.anchor: bu abd-i hakīri ve bunları hüsn-i nazarla okuyup ona hayırhah olanları

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing supplication asks God for a tranquil soul that believes in meeting Him, accepts His decree, and is content with His gift.
rows.anchor: نـَفْسًا مُطْمَئِنَّةً تـُؤْمِنُ بِلِقَائِكَ وَتـَرْضَى بِقَضَائِكَ
